utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. Before we call the case, may I ask Dr. Stakic in person, how do you feel today, and are you able to follow the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can say that I feel somewhat better than I did yesterday, but not altogether well. As far as I can tell as a person and as a doctor, I believe that I am just tired. I have been stressed for a long time, and I believe that a rest of three to five days would help me. But in order to help this -- these proceedings and because the witnesses are here, I'll do my best and I'll keep on going. And then we will have a few days off. And I believe that during that period of time, I will be able to rest. I am very sorry that because we have to work for the whole day, I don't get the chance to go out to get some fresh air. I have problems with the diet, and as time goes on, this accumulates and the weekend is not long enough to help me recuperate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this statement, Dr. Stakic. I'll come back immediately to this question, but now the time is ripe to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. As the parties know, but also the public should know, we had a 65 ter (i) meeting yesterday discussing a long range of outstanding issues. I don't want to repeat what can be read as soon as possible from the minutes, but you can see we started later today, and this was due to the fact that we had some deliberations in the Chamber. And a clear statement should be given in the direction of both parties. The Judges of this Trial Chamber will no longer accept a policy of obstruction as shown by both parties from the outset in this case. The Chamber also in future will only be guided by the statute. The statute demands that the Trial Chamber shall ensure that the trial is fair and expeditious. The conclusions: Yesterday, it was agreed that the Defence case should be, as envisaged, concluded no later than the 21st of March, 2003. However, we take into account that both parties do not appreciate all the attempts to give additional time in this case for the Defence. I know the underlying reasons, and I can understand the position of Dr. Stakic himself, who has, no doubt, special problems emanating from the fact that when a case is heard both in the morning and in the afternoon, unfortunately the bureaucracy is not able to give you the possibility and give you what is your right under the Rules, namely, one hour of movement in the fresh air and to provide the necessary food for you. So therefore, we take it -- we can't understand the position taken by the Prosecution, but for the reasons given especially related to Dr. Stakic, we take it that in future, in principle, there will be only hearing either in the mornings or in the afternoons as of the 3rd of March only. It was, however, agreed that we sit today and from the 17th to 21 February as previously scheduled. This will be in the morning and in the first part of the afternoon. In the interest of the witnesses already having arrived in The Hague and Dr. Stakic himself mentioned this, and I appreciate this comment, in the interest of these witnesses, we'll try to finalise the hearing of the witnesses during this week. But if this could not be or would not be possibly, we would continue Monday, the 10th of February as scheduled. But in any event, there will be no hearings Tuesday, the 11th of February, the 12th of February, as previously fixed as United Nations holidays, through the 14th of February, day of courtroom maintenance. I hope this will facilitate your situation, Dr. Stakic. The Defence announced that they would move for the hearing of up to 24 witnesses under Rule 92 bis opposed to two witnesses being currently under this rule on the witness list. Taking into account that the OTP has a right to respond and presiding officer has to be appointed by the Registrar of the Tribunal, for that purpose under Rule 92(B) and the procedure under Rule 92 bis, preparation and implementation, will take a lot of time, we hereby rearrange the deadline for this motion under 92 bis from the 3rd of March to the 17th of February. Only this allows us to continue as scheduled. Just this morning, we received the motion on the appointment of a presiding officer, but the order of the motion, no doubt, has to be the following, that first we have a clear list of these witnesses to be heard under Rule 92 bis. Then it's the right for the Prosecution to respond, hopefully as soon as possible and practicable. And only then we can continue with the question of the appointment on all the practical measures to be taken, first of all, by the Registrar. Furthermore, regarding the schedule, following rebuttal and rejoinder, there will be first, as agreed yesterday, a day dedicated to deliberations, as we did it before the 98 bis decision in order to direct the parties to the core issues the Chamber as such has identified, be it on legal issues, be it on factual issues. This will be then followed by exchange of oral arguments. The final brief should arrive with the Bench as soon as possible, but no later than Thursday, the 10th of April. In the direction of the Prosecution, we deeply deplore the approach taken by the Prosecution. From our position, it is not possible to proceed in the same way as it was done in the past. And I know that the addressee of my words is not present in the courtroom. I think no Prosecutor in the entire world has the right to proceed, to continue the Prosecution, knowing that a person presumed innocent will -- that there will be no evidence enough or that in part incidents never will be proven and even charges can no longer be continued. To continue proceedings against a person whom the Prosecution knows that they are no longer able to proceed under the Rules and not able to establish the case could amount to an unfair treatment. Why this? Because it demands from the Defence to cover all the charges, all the incidents, and all the accidents described in the fourth amended indictment. And I hope that the Prosecution is aware that in part they can't prove some of these accusations, be it for legal reasons, be it for factual reasons. Therefore, it would be more than appropriate, and we hereby invite de Novo, I don't know whether it's the fifth or the tenth time, the Prosecution to do the necessary under the Rules, to slimline the case and reduce it to that what really can be the outcome of the case, taking into account the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. As mentioned in the statute, we are mandated to ensure that the trial is not only fair, but also expeditious. And the behaviour shown by the Prosecution in the past - and once again, I apologise because the representative of the Prosecution responsible for this is not in the moment in this courtroom - brings us in a situation that, in fact, the Defence has to do more than necessary. We only want to start this attempt to limit the relevant areas to be covered by giving the judicial hint that the question, if so, why Dr. Stakic decided to move to Belgrade is absolutely irrelevant for the outcome of this case. Evidence related to this question will be no longer admissible. And I hope we can continue and I hope that we will have more and better cooperation with the Prosecution in the future. And this only enables us to limit the area what is relevant for this case and only this enables the Trial Chamber to do that what the Trial Chamber is mandated for, a fair and expeditious trial. And but this right is not only the right of Dr. Stakic, but also the right of other persons in the Detention Unit spending there up to three years without a concrete date when their case will start. We have to balance all these interests, and I hope that in the future, there will be a better cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if Your Honour wishes us to respond or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think in the interest of the waiting witness and in the interest of all the witnesses, this should be done at a later point of time when the parties had the possibility to rethink their approach. This is a question related to both parties, but it's absolutely necessary to rearrange the upcoming hearings. And in future, we will concentrate that only relevant evidence will be heard in this courtroom. That's in the interest of all the parties, and it's in the interest of the other persons in the Detention Unit. So whenever the parties believe it's appropriate, please let me know, and then we'll discuss this in depth. Maybe it's appropriate to do this after the break of next week. For the witness today, and this is the only question we have before us now, anything has to be said before we ask the witness to enter the courtroom? I can't see anything. May I therefore ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. Yesterday, we provisionally marked the documents D66 to D69. May I ask the Prosecution, what about objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore admitted into evidence under these numbers. The English version as "a"; the B/C/S version as "b."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. And thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience. I have to apologise that you had to wait such a long time for unforeseeable reasons, but let's hope that we can continue and maybe even conclude your testimony. So may I ask to continue with the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, Mr. Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you yesterday whether you knew who supplied the petrol station with fuel, with petrol, and who was in charge of the petrol station in the summer of 1992. I think we have managed to clarify this point. Now I'd like to ask you something about the kitchen. We started talking about this. The kitchen was near part of your facilities in the so-called Separacija, separation. In the summer of 1992, did your enterprise supply this kitchen with the goods necessary for cooking meals, meals that were distributed to the army and to detainees at the Omarska investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The kitchen at Omarska is part of the administration building. The so-called iron ore mine complex, the separation is near the railway station. When you enter the administration building, the kitchen is to the left. And to the right, you have a flight of stairs leading to the first floor of the administration building. I'm trying to prevent any misunderstanding concerning the spatial disposition of these rooms, so that's as far as the so-called separation area is concerned. The kitchen was designed to cater for the shifts working at the iron ore mine. All the goods needed to produce the meals, to cook the meals, were brought there from the central storage in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This kitchen near the administration building was also there during the operation of the investigation centre, but do you know that food was actually -- meals were actually not cooked in that particular kitchen during the operation of the investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. Essentially since the 20th something of May, and after the momentous and unfortunate incidents that took place, I had no relation to Omarska, and I simply don't know who supplied the kitchen with the necessary goods nor who worked in the kitchen. I don't know where the meals were prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you about events after September 1992. Do you know anything about the attempts to remove Dr. Stakic from his position, and do you know where those particular Municipal Assembly sessions were held?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In earlier times, assembly sessions were held at the so-called workers' council hall. That was in the headquarters of the Ljubija iron ore mine. That's also where my offices were -- where my office was at that period of time. That's on the ground floor of that building. And this workers' council hall can seat about 250 people taking part in any of the meetings taking place there. The huge capacity of this particular hall is one of the reasons the meetings, the sessions, were held there. As for the assembly, and I did know some of those people, they were members of the SDS, and there was a belligerent group, a belligerent faction there, a group of people who weren't happy with the assembly's work up to that point. They weren't happy with the way Dr. Stakic led the assembly, chaired the assembly. Dusan Kurnoga was among those people. He was a member of that particular group. There was also a man called Sidjak whose first name I can't remember. Another man, Zmijanjac, again, I can't remember his first name. I think this group probably enjoyed the support of the president of the SDS, Simo Miskovic. I can't recall the exact date when this session took place in the hall. But I know that my director of technical services was a member of the SDS, and he attended the meeting. He would go in and out, but he attended part of the meeting. His name is Slobodan Balaban. He informed me that demands had been made for Dr. Stakic's removal, but no consensus could be reached. And they decided to keep the assembly in permanent ongoing session. So they stayed there for the whole day and the following night. It was their opinion that they should take, take over the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior. I don't know what the reasons were for that, but I later found out that I, too, was to be arrested in the cellar. I don't know what the final result of the session was, how the session ended. But for a period of time following the session, there were a number of removals taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When these removals were taking place, did members of this group you've just told us about take up positions from which they had previously removed people?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Their main idea was that the SDS had power, but had no money. It was for this reason that they wanted 12 managing directors of state-owned enterprises removed from office. I was one of the people who were blacklisted. In Prijedor, in the Energopetrol company, they had Radomir Bursac removed and appointed Mr. Sidjak whom I have referred to a moment ago. I can't remember his first name. At the post office, at the post office company in Prijedor, they had Mr. Marko Pavic removed. This was where they stopped. I have no idea why they decided to call it a day at that point. But I do know that Mr. Sidjak, over the months that followed, embezzled in some way or expropriated in Belgrade approximately 450.000 German marks. He was later convicted for that crime. I'm not sure how long the sentence was, but he did spend time in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When this group took up their new positions, the positions of previously held by people they removed from those very positions, did this group manage to take over the MUP?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Simo Drljaca took up the position of the deputy -- I'm not sure exactly what the position was officially called. But he was to be the first man of the Republika Srpska MUP with headquarters at Bijeljina. However, he was not replaced by Zmijanjac, as had been planned, but if I remember correctly, the man who replaced him was Delic. I can't remember Delic's first name. And I can't remember how long Delic stayed in that position. I know that he was to return. I know that Simo Drljaca was at a later point to return to his old position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that Simo Drljaca left and took up position as a deputy, did he go to Bijeljina at that time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was supposed to be based in Bijeljina, his office should have been in Bijeljina. I have information that he spent quite some time in Novi Sad. What was the reason for his stay in Novi Sad, I really don't know. But he would turn up in Prijedor, too, and quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that a promotion or a demotion for Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a person is first the chief of the MUP of Prijedor and then leaves to take up the position of a deputy or an assistant - I'm not sure what the official title of the position was - well, that should be considered a promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This group you referred to as belligerent or militant, the group that had Dr. Stakic and some other people removed, did they ever succeed in establishing any form of control over the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late 1993, when I became the vice-president of the Executive Board, Mr. Kurnoga was still in his position as the president of the municipality. My appointment -- I said that the one condition for my appointment and my acceptance of that appointment was that Kurnoga resign. The SDS leadership promised me this, but they never fulfilled that promise. Therefore, I feel entitled to add a comment to your question. It is my opinion, and I am convinced, that regardless of the militancy and arrogance of that group, there would have been no way for them to give orders to either the army or the MUP for the simple reason that the structure, according to the then-existing laws -- the MUP is quite literally independent in terms of hierarchy, the chief of the Prijedor MUP at that time would have answered to Banja Luka, that is, to Bijeljina and vice versa. They were the commanders of the Prijedor MUP. As for the army, they also worked according to the old laws and regulations. In the former Yugoslavia, they were directly under the command of the presidency, and in the Republika Srpska I assume the situation was the same. They would have been under the command of the presidency. And regardless of the fact that that group of lads wanted radical change and more power for themselves, it is my submission that they had no authority to issue any orders to the MUP or to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another question: Please tell us, if you know, the army or the police, did they get their salaries from the municipality or from the republic or, in the case of the army, from the federative state -- federal state prior to that period?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain about the army --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Again, it's vague as to time that we're talking about, and counsel said "prior to that period." I'm not sure what period he's asking the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question regarding the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the creation of the army of Republika Srpska, who paid the salaries of the military? Who did the military receive their salaries from until the beginning of May 1992? And if you know, could you please tell us after the beginning of May 1992, who did the army receive their salaries from? And also, if you know about 1991, 1992, and later who the police received their salaries from.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six questions in one. I'll try to deal with all of them. Please excuse the boldness of my remark. I will try to give an answer as accurate as I can. I am certain that the army was paid and supplied from the budget of the former Yugoslavia or from the republic budget. They did have a number of privileges for the same reason. That's prior to 1992. The same system continued in 1992 -- 1991, 1992, 1993, and probably even after that. I must point out in 1994, there was a situation that represented a slight aberration from what I was telling you about. The Executive Board in 1994 secured part of the budget, funds from part of the budget, for the families of soldiers who had been on the front. I think this can be traced in the documents of the Municipal Assembly. As for the MUP, I don't think I can give you a precise answer. I suppose that were probably paid from the budget, but I know that the MUP was not paid from the municipal budget in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are coming to the end of my direct examination. I would now like to ask you whether you know Dr. Stakic; when was it that you met him; and can you please tell us how well you know him.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. I know Dr. Stakic. I heard of him sometime in 1991 when the assembly -- the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor was being set up, and I was wondering about the fact that somebody who was not known in Prijedor would appear in the assembly. At that point in time, I didn't know him. I had only heard that he was a doctor. But there were a number of physicians in the political life at that time. In late 1991 and early 1992, we finally met. I believe that at that time, he was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. To be honest, when I first went to see him, I expected somebody stronger, somebody taller, and then I met somebody who was of my height, and I'm not very tall, who was very pleasant. And later on, he told me that he came from the family of Stakics who lived to the south of the surface excavation ground in Omarska. And while I was the leader of the project in Omarska from 1974 to 1979, we had to expropriate some land for the disposal site in Javori. And then I remembered the family that Dr. Stakic belonged to, especially his father. I even think that his father is the same age as me. We had some problems with the expropriation of the land from some of the people there, but Dr. Stakic's father was really very good about that. We didn't have any problems with him regardless of the fact that this disposal site later on had to be moved partly to the land of the Stakic family that hadn't been expropriated in the first stage. We had to do that because of the weather conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Thank you for the answer. But I just need clarification. Did you expect to find a stronger or a more heavily built man, or did you expect to see somebody who would be a stronger person in terms of his personality? Did you expect a different, a stronger personality, or just a strongly built person?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, during that period of time, people who appeared in certain positions were behaving, I would say, with a degree of arrogance and who were -- who had the traits of the person who couldn't control the power that were given to them. That's how I also imagined I would find Dr. Stakic. But I have already said that later on when I had to work with him, and we did not have the opportunity to socialise a lot. But in any case, I realised that he was just the opposite of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dr. Stakic on television? Did you ever hear him on a radio delivering a speech?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, never. I never heard him on radio or on television. At least during the time when I listened to Radio Prijedor and watched television, I don't know if he appeared outside the time when I followed the media. I didn't see his interviews in Kozarski Vjesnik because I don't read Kozarski Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why don't you read Kozarski Vjesnik, Mr. Marjanovic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the Prijedor paper which, to my mind, does not have to be correct. There is around it some journalists who are not responsible, who are not really professionals in their work, and the paper that they printed contained a lot of gossip, a lot of unverified information. So there was a lack of professionalism. There was ignorance about the subject matter that they were writing about. I'm not saying that all the journalists were like that, but I believe the lady whose name is Jadranka Recevic was an example of somebody who wrote interviews and articles under the influence of alcohol. And she was not the only one there. That's why I didn't read the Kozarski Vjesnik. And the only truth that could be found in Kozarski Vjesnik was in obituaries on the last pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would the usher be so kind and show the witness Exhibit Number S374, please. I think that the letters are too small for the gentleman to read. So if the B/C/S version could be put on the ELMO and enlarged so it would be able maybe to... And, Your Honour, this exhibit is actually for a different article But I would like the witness to read a new text with the name "The production started in northern Tomasica." [Interpretation] "The production started in northern Tomasica." [In English] And it's on the bottom half on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the transcript, date of this issue of the newspaper would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would be August 14th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, can you please move the paper the way it suits you so that you are able to read it. Are you able to read this?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would it be better if I read and Mr. Marjanovic just follows, Your Honour, if it's too hard for him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No problem. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May it be noted that the interpreters do not have that in the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do we have another copy for the booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's on the screen, so they might follow on the screen as well. And maybe the technical booth can have the whole body of the text --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I am willing to give up my copy since I can't understand it anyway. I think the B/C/S will be helpful. This is not I presume on -- you can also have it -- if it's on the Defence 65 ter list, we would have another copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's wait a minute until the booth has the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like the technical booth just to zoom out a bit. That's okay. I think -- a bit to zoom in. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we can -- difficult to identify, but I think the booths are ready. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Good news from Ljubija. The production of iron ore starts in Sjeverna Tomasica after a two-month interruption due to the war operations. Heavy mechanisation is again working in Ljubija. Last Friday, the excavation sites in Tomasica again produced the iron ore that results in the production of quality dyes that have their application in the production of varnishes and dyes. "The activation of this mining production is of multifold significance. It will meet the needs of the factory of natural iron oxides which operates as a segment of the Ljubija mine, and it will enable exports to the market of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Since the payment transactions have still not been organised with the countries of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, it is with a good reason that Ljubija wishes for the barter deal to be clinched so that they can get oil in return for their production. That would put in place the condition of the production of a hundred tonnes of dyes for a larger export to the markets of Germany. "It is interesting that the management board and the experts of our largest producer of iron ore do not want to stay just on the production of iron ore and delivery of dyes. Since in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is no factory which would produce the same range of products, the construction of the factory of dyes in Busnovi would be a good business move. This is corroborated by the fact that there are already facilities and infrastructure, but there's no equipment which is lacking because of the lack of foreign currency. But this problem can be solved. The sheet-based Hepra, a business partner of the Ljubija mine is ready to give them the production line under certain conditions, and this deal is now almost completed. "This is not, however, the only investment programme of the Ljubija mine, but we shall bring you more about that in the next issue of Kozarski Vjesnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am going to read the last sentence to you once again. "However, this is not the only investment project of the Ljubija mine, but we shall bring you more about that in the next issue of Kozarski Vjesnik." Was at the time northern Tomasica a part of the Ljubija mine? And can you please tell us whether there was a transformation; and if there was, when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please give me the date of this Kozarski Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was the 14th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try to give you some more detail on this, given the fact that what it says here is not correct. But I'll try and explain. On the 1st of February, 1991, I became the CEO of the Ljubija mine and I presented my programme of creating a holding company. That was the reason why I was appointed, why I was chosen to be the CEO. Throughout 1991, based on the data that I had from the Cajevec factory Banja Luka which was incepted as a holding and of some other companies, I believed that the solution of that kind was bad and I decided that some parts of the Ljubija mine should be shared off, especially those parts that could work independently and who -- which were able to appear on the market with their range of products independently of the Ljubija mine. The Ferox factory in the eastern part of Tomasica started producing in 1986 or 1987. And it was constructed as a joint venture with Litostroj from Ljubljana, and it had Japanese technology. The reason why it was constructed was the excavation site in the eastern part of Tomasica in geological terms, it was a sedimented excavation site of homolytic iron ore where the particles are -- homolytic particles were of micron size. There were two variants of the dye, the yellow dye and the brown dye. Such natural pigments are very rare anywhere in the world. And the thickness and the amount of pigment was about 4 and a half million tonnes in the eastern part of Tomasica. That's why the fabric was constructed, and that's why it started producing with a capacity of 10.000 tonnes a year. And it was one of the parts of the Ljubija iron ore mine. It sold its product to the factories of varnishes and dyes as a filler. We started to -- we tried to start the production of the black pigment, but -- because we could sell it in Sweden and in Australia. So the factory had a closed technology, they had a market, and they had raw materials. That's why I decided that they should be made independent and that they should be incepted as an independent economic subject and registered in the commercial court. They left the Ljubija mine in early 1992, and this article, as you said, was printed in August. And I believe that any comment would be superfluous, and it really illustrates the professionalism of the journalist who authored this article -- actually, the author didn't sign this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have 10 or 15 minutes, and if it would be a convenient time for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, but before having the break, I have to announce that the motion related to five witnesses to take their testimony with the assistance of a videolink is granted in principle. A written decision will follow immediately, just in order that the Registry can already now take the necessary steps for preparing these videolinks. But it shouldn't be forgotten that in case, be it the other party or be it the Bench, has the impression that it would be necessary to hear the one or the other witness as a live witness, there is still the option to come back to this witness and hear this witness live. As to the fact that the motion from 4 February, 2003, asking for the appointment of a presiding officer under Rule 92 bis and that this motion is called "urgent" and it calls for an instant or immediate answer, and we have to point out that before we can decide on this, no doubt, we need the names and the reasons for why you believe that those statements would be those falling under Rule 90 bis(A) especially. The standard is, of course, not as we can read it from your motion, that due to the fact that the Court has admitted approximately 19 written statements offered by the OTP pursuant to Rule 92 bis, it would follow from this that now the same number of witnesses have to be admitted under 92 bis with their statements in return. We are bound by Rule 92 bis, and we have to find out whether or whether or not these witnesses fall in the purview of Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could briefly respond, in order for us to respond to the motion on 92 bis, we need to know what the statements are going to say. And we -- at the moment, we don't have it. When the Defence had to respond to our motions, we had written signed statements from each of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this assistance. That's just what I wanted to point out. Because the parametres can be found in Rule 92 bis(A), and we have not the slightest idea what the name and what should be in the statement of these envisaged 24 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll use the next week to go in the field and to finalise this part of our job. But if necessary, now, we can provide some names and general topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We gave the deadline, and we stated "as soon as possible," but no later than the 17th of February. So during this period of time, I think it's not necessary to do the -- or to prepare the statements and to announce all of the -- the contents of all of the statements you expect to have from the witnesses. But if you could start at least as there was an invitation from the side of the Prosecution already in the past, you could proceed step by step. This would already assist because you should be aware, when we receive your motion, including the names and the factors necessary to decide whether or not it is admissible under Rule 92 bis, it will take time for the Prosecution to respond. It will take time for the Registrar to take the necessary measures. And no doubt, it will take time to hear these witnesses and to take the statements as foreseen under Rule 92 bis(B). So therefore, in the moment, we can't decide on your motion from yesterday requesting the appointment of a presiding officer because apparently this is the second step and we expect the first step. Nothing else has to be added in the moment. The trial stays adjourned until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like the usher to show the witness exhibit marked S107, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask in the meantime, the Defence is tendering the last article of Kozarski Vjesnik, because previously we only admitted another article.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From the same page. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then admitted as D70B. And it should be mentioned in the list of exhibits that we can find the translation on today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, yesterday, or the day before yesterday, you mentioned this document. This is a document allegedly signed by Simo Drljaca. On the last page of this document, it says: "Delivered among others also to the managing director of the iron ore mine Ljubija." We'll go through this document, and you will tell us if this document was ever delivered to you and if you are the person of whom it is stated here that on the 30th of May, 1992, was the general manager of the Ljubija iron ore mines. Will you please read item 1.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The provisional collection centre for persons captured in combat or detained on the grounds of the security services operation, the industrial compound of the Omarska mine strip mine shall serve as a provisional collection centre for persons captured in combat or on the grounds of the security services operation."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please read out number 7 now.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The mine's management shall organise meals for investigators, guards, and detainees according to norms established in agreement with the quartermaster service. At the same time, the mine's management shall organise the regular cleaning as well as maintenance of plumbing, electrical fixtures, and other utilities. It shall also ensure other kinds of logistical support for the work and stay of the given number of persons on the given premises by imposing obligatory work on skilled employees."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was: If your company was in charge of organising the meals, you said you did not supply anything for the preparation of these meals?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my responsible submission that we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if your workers were in charge of maintaining the plumbing and electrical fixtures, and was it done pursuant to this decision or in a different way?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document bears the date 31st of May, 1992. I must say that contacts with people in Omarska were becoming very infrequent during May following the events in Kozarac. So my comments will refer to the period preceding these events. The duties of people from the surroundings of the mines, the reason we did this, is to make it easier for them to find jobs. A number of people worked on maintaining the well and the water well. Some people were maintenance workers on the pumps and the surface excavations. There were people working as security officers, too. Excuse me, can you please repeat the question. This means I cannot make a claim to this effect simply because I had no information. But I assume that they continued in their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Item 8 reads: "The management shall without delay fence off the compound around the management building with barbed wire, placing a barrier on the road to Omarska, and shall also provide drinking water. The guards shall prevent any unauthorised persons from approaching or entering the collection centre in accordance with the official guard-duty rules." Do you know or did you hear whether this centre, this complex, was ever surrounded with barbed wire?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know, nor did I hear anything about that. Even after 1996 when I did go to Omarska, I saw no traces of anything like that. The barrier, I don't see what the purpose of a barrier would have been because there is a gate when you go from Omarska to the mine. There is a gate through which you enter the mining complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if this barrier was actually ever set up? Did you ever see it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are several other requests or orders here that were purportedly delivered to the managers of the mines. However, items 10 and 14 also refer to the mine's management. It says that "The mine management shall in collaboration with the chief of security and chief of security services coordinators make available the maintenance and repair shops and office space in collaboration with the security chief and security service coordinators in the interests of greater efficiency should it prove necessary." And item 14: "The mine's managers and management shall select reliable and qualified personnel for assignment to duties required of them at the collection centre. They cannot replace them unless absolutely necessary and with the approval of the public security station. The management shall send a list of all appointed staff members to the public security station in Prijedor without delay." The question I would like to ask you, again, the last page and the list of addressees, the list of people this document was allegedly delivered to, number 6, the director of RZR Ljubija, does that mean you? Are you the person under number 6?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should seem obvious, but I could also say that I'm not because my official title in that period was the president of the business board of the Ljubija iron ore mines. But if it reads "Ljubija iron ore mines," that is the complex association of associated labour, so that would indicate that I was the person under number 6. But my comment, and I say this with full responsibility, I have never seen this document and I was not familiar with this document. Some days ago, when you showed the document to me was the first time I laid eyes on it, and I believe I've said this before. If this had ever reached me, I don't think I would be here now to testify before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why do you say that, that you would not be here now to testify?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not allow -- I wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or would you have tried to prevent it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I simply wouldn't have allowed it for that very reason. I really don't know how the whole thing would have ended. Item 14 says a lot about it. It's very eloquent. It says that the public security station, if I understand right, insists on qualified and double-checked workers and wants a list delivered. It is quite obvious that the public security station took all the matters into their hands. I did not provide any lists. And if this had been delivered to me, I'm absolutely certain this would have been recorded in the protocol of the Ljubija iron ore mines which was mandatory for our legal section. They would have had to record this. I'd like to comment on the last page, if I may. There's a handwritten bit which says -- that's if I see right -- received on behalf of Mica [as interpreted] iron ore mines and security. I'm not familiar with either of these signatures. Obviously, my conclusion is that this circulated from person to person privately and unofficially. This was not officially delivered, which means that this decision could never have reached me anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. May I ask you, what stands this abbreviation for M-u-i-c? You just read "received on behalf of Muic, Muic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand this correctly, the handwriting reads: "Received on behalf of Mijic, iron ore mines." So you asked me about the meaning of the word Mijic. Under number 1, you have Crisis Staff, coordinators of the security services. And there you see the last name Mijic, last name Mesic, and Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic. So I suppose the handwriting part refers to this gentleman named Mijic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And this Mr. Mijic, he was employed in the iron ore mines at all, or do you know this person or a person with the name Mijic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say that Mr. Mijic was not an employee of the iron ore mines if you look at this text, coordinators of the security services, which means that he was an employee of the security services. I do know a man, and I suppose this refers to him. I know a man named Mijic who worked in the public security centre. I know this man by sight. We didn't have any personal contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If I may -- it may be that a person works for one institution and at the same time for another. To the best of your recollection, was a Mr. Mijic employed within the iron ore mines company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speaking about the last name itself, I cannot claim that there was not a single person named Mijic working at the iron ore mines. We had 4.630 employees. But if we're talking about the person who worked for the security services, if we're talking about that particular person, then it is my submission that he was at no time ever employed as a worker at the iron ore mines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution has asked for the floor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I thought it might be helpful to Your Honours to remind Your Honours that the evidence is that this document was seized from the Prijedor police station, and also refer to the testimony of Mr. Jankovic where Mr. Mijic is referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are aware of this. I think we should make use of the witness before us, and I think that you are here that you can testify to the best of your knowledge. So please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember Mr. Mijic's first name?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said you never received this document, and you added had you received this, you wouldn't be here to testify here today because you would have stood up against it. Do you think someone would have killed you for that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so. And the period of time I'm talking about, between May and until the 5th or the 10th of June, within that period of time, everything was possible. Nothing was to be ruled out. All the more because - and I'm speaking about myself now - I was not really Mr. Drljaca's favorite. He didn't like me that much, you know. I refused to meet his requests concerning passes for the workers of the iron ore mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you not meet his requests concerning passes or did you not meet any of his other requests aside from the requests concerning passes?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I need to correct myself. I was obliged to meet his requests concerning passes because there was maintenance work on the pumps to be done as well as matters concerning the security guards at the iron ore mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, you did say this the first time around, but that's not what the transcript reflected. Briefly, before we conclude, I would like to ask you the following: Do you know whether the president of the Municipal Assembly is superior to the secretary of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe not. I am convinced not. The secretary is an official functionary. He is elected by the assembly, and he is in charge of tasks of legal nature as a secretary of the assembly for the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The section for common or shared services of the Municipal Assembly, are they subordinated to the secretary or do they have their own chief?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to explain this. There was the secretariat for general affairs, which also included staff such as drivers, secretaries, cleaning ladies. There is another section which deals with legal matters. It's a body of the assembly working on materials or requests, incoming requests, from anyone, requests from the Executive Board, from state organs. I was not, myself, president of the municipality, but I don't think that even the secretary would have been directly subordinated to the president of the Municipal Assembly. The president of the Municipal Assembly has no authority to give any orders, even to any of the secretaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say you attended some of the duty sessions of the Crisis Staff, but you also say that you never attended any of their meetings. Did you ever at any single point during these duty sessions of the Crisis Staff notice that they were receiving reports from the army, from the police, or that they were issuing orders to the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may please just have the screen blank so that I could join in when the interpreters finish interpreting. Thank you. I believe I did say before that I did attend several of these so-called duty sessions in the Crisis Staff. I think I even explained where the office was in which this took place. Perhaps I may add now that people from the iron ore mines brought food in for those on duty. I would be there between 8.00 and 11.00 or 12.00. I hardly ever stayed later than that. During that particular period, I am sure that those people were not receiving any reports or giving any orders. I think I've said this before, too. The nature of their work was civilian in the very sense of the word. Citizens would come and complain about shortages of water, electricity, utility problem, that sort of thing. I claim with full responsibility that during the time I spent there, there were no incoming reports or documents from the MUP or the army, nor did any people from the MUP or the army ever come there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you draw any conclusions from the telephone calls and conversations that people on duty were making if they had any contacts with the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a rather small office, so of course I did overhear conversations of those present in the office. I'll give you one example, just in order to illustrate this. I think Mr. Kovacevic was on duty, and the party called. On the basis of his answer, I assumed that the question was about water, about shortage of water, and if they had water at that point. What he answered is: "Just open the spout and see if any water comes out." If I was in a position to hear what he was saying, then of course I would have been in a position to hear everyone else. For example, Mr. Budimir when he was on duty. I heard no conversations at all with either the army or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Marjanovic. This concludes our examination-in-chief. Now you will be asked questions by my colleagues from the Prosecution and after that by the Honourable Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, please, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, referring to the document that you were shown - we don't need to put it back - about the Omarska mine, you indicated that if you had seen that document, you probably would be dead. And I understand your answer to be because you would not have allowed it. And your answer on page 26 was "No, I simply wouldn't have allowed it." Can you explain what would you have not allowed.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not have agreed with such a document. I would not have approved this document, and I claim with full responsibility that things would have happened in the same way despite my approval or disapproval. But bearing in mind my relationship with Mr. Simo Drljaca who did not -- who could not take a refusal of an order, later on he threatened to hang me. And this did not happen. And it was just my assumption. I didn't say that for a fact, but I'm sure that I would not have agreed with a request and the content of such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We'll come back to your relationship with Mr. Drljaca later. But my question for you now, sir, is: What would you not have allowed? Is it your testimony that you would not have allowed the facilities and personnel that came under your supervision to take part in the Omarska camp in the location where prisoners were detained?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances, if one wanted to enter the compound of the mine, one had to have the approval of the management of the mine. In this case, I would have not given my approval for the things that are indicated in this document. I would also have tried to protect my people who were there. And again, I claim nobody ever asked me, I never saw this document, and nobody ever gave me an opportunity to voice my protests about that. If my memory serves me well, under item number 14, one could read that the MUP had taken over the role of both the person issuing the request and the person carrying out that request or following that request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I understand your testimony, sir, you're indicating that the reason you did not oppose the use of the mine facilities and personnel was because you never received this document, although you're listed as an addressee? You never saw it before coming to The Hague this week. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the document, and my conclusion based on the document as I have seen it now is what I have already said, that if I had received the document at that time, I would have acted in the way I have told you I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, didn't you testify that you were aware of the mine being taken over by the army in May? Let me ask you: Weren't you aware in May that the army did what you described as a takeover of the Omarska mine?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the end of May. I believe it was around 27th or the 28th of May. I don't know the exact date. I once said that this had happened at that time because of the events in Kozarac and other things, one could not get to Omarska. I didn't go there. And I must add to that the fact that in the work of the mine, the subordination of the head of every particular plant is of all sorts. And at that time, the director of the Omarska plant was Dusko Vlacina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, are you denying that you were responsible as, in your position as the CEO of Ljubija mines, for the facilities and for the personnel of the Omarska mine, that they came under your supervision?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can my learned friend specify the time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it was quite clear the time period the Prosecution is relating to in the moment. The witness himself spoke about the 27 to 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim with full responsibility that after the events which took place in Kozarac, I did not have any instruments at my disposal. I did not have any possibility to exert any influence on what was going on in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let's go to the period in April 1992. The Omarska facility fell under your management. You were the top manager of the Omarska facility and the other assets of the Ljubija mine company. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us that you became aware from security guards, I believe you told us - I'm looking for the page but I can't find it - that the army and police had entered the facility in late May. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, at that time did you put your life on the line and oppose the takeover of the Omarska mine in order to turn it into a camp for the citizens of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say, and I have already said it a little while ago, that during those misfortunate events, I did not have any instruments at my disposal that would help me to do that. I was at home. I was looking after my own family. As of the 27th or 28th of May up to 25th or 26th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, who did you complain to about the takeover of the assets of the company that you were in charge of, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go to anybody because I repeat once again, I did not have any instruments at my disposal that would help me do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want to take advantage of your experience and expertise regarding mining in the Prijedor municipality, particularly I believe you told us that you worked on the Omarska project for about five years. Is that correct? And you are very familiar with that facility. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have stated here that I was the leader of the project Omarska between 1974 and 1979. We were in charge of the design and the feasibility study of Omarska. Maybe I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The design first of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and if counsel or the Court feel it's necessary to continue the explanation, but my question is really not regarding those details, sir. I'm just asking, are you familiar -- in 1992, were you familiar with the Omarska facility?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have started my explanation about that, and this would have been the answer to your question. Based on the design and the feasibility study, the facilities are constructed, the final construction was after the final design was drawn up. So yes, I do have a rough idea about what the facilities in Omarska look like. I can tell you that there is a gate on the left-hand side of the administrative building of the separation. On the right-hand side, there are warehouses, and then there is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir. Thank you. And I don't mean to interrupt you again, and I'm sorry I did before. But we have photographs and are familiar with the layout. Thank you for your answer. Can you tell the Court why, based upon your knowledge of the Omarska facility, why that would be a particularly suitable facility - would you agree with me - particularly suitable facility for a prison camp, especially for a camp where dead bodies would have to be disposed of?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness is asked to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I briefly respond before the Court confers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness gave testimony about the powers of the municipal president, the army, the police, which he has no direct knowledge of. He is the owner of the mine. He's a mining expert. So I'm asking him a question directly related to his expertise, not the owner but the manager, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objection dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, based on your knowledge of Prijedor, Omarska, and the events of 1992, why do you think the Omarska facility was chosen for the prisoner camp?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say that I am an expert in mining. I note that there is about a hundred million tonnes of iron ore lying there, and as to your question about the choice of that site, I can't really provide you with an answer. I don't understand your question. How can I, as a mining expert, say why is this site suitable for an investigation centre or, as you call it, a camp. I cannot give you a comment on that because to -- in my mind, regardless of what happened there, there's no place for thinking about it, for any way to think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, was the Omarska facility located a significant distance - I believe you testified about 20 kilometres - from the town of Prijedor with the nearest villages being villages that were predominantly of Serbian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just said is all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did the Omarska facility have heavy equipment, including heavy trucks, and mining equipment such as digging equipment at its disposal?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have already said it here when we were talking about the transportation means, and I can repeat it if I have to. A mine like this usually has heavy equipment started with EKG, 346 Russian-made excavators, and rotor excavators made in Germany, then bandwagons made in Germany, Crips [phoen] crushers at the excavation site. And as for lorries, it has dumpers of 75 tonnes carriage capacity made by Caterpillar. Then Ranke [phoen] 75 tonnes capacity. Those were all American trucks. Then there were bulldozers also made by Caterpillar. And all this is equipment that serves for the exploitation of the iron ore in Omarska and in Ljubija in general. And other excavation sites had similar equipment. But in Omarska, there's also the gravitation magnetic separation technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Before I move on, sir, I want to make sure I understand your positions with the mine company. You were appointed in February of 1991 as the CEO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President of the management board and it is correct that it was on the 1st of February, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 1990s, there was the process of erosion of the economy in the Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was a lack of cash. There were strikes. And there was a collective resignation of the management board in late 1990. And there was an opening for the position of the manager, and there was a need to appoint a new manager, a new president of the management board. I applied together with two other candidates, and a committee was set up by the workers' council consisting of three members, one of them was a mining engineer, one was of them was an economist, and one had a degree in law. The committee was in charge of reviewing obligations. The review and their decision was presented to the workers' council which consisted over 60 members. There was a long debate which lasted over a year and a half and finally members of the workers' council reached a unanimous decision, and I was appointed the president of the management board after this long discussion which lasted for over one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Until what time did you serve in that position, or do you continue to serve in that position?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer your first or your second question? I can give you the correct answer to both. I was in the position of the president of the management board until the beginning of 1992. And then the company disintegrated. Some of its parts were shed off. I was talking about that earlier this morning when I was talking about the pigments and about the article that we read. After that, my position was the general director of the mine, but in order to avoid a confusion, the mine that remained as such had three production plants and several sectors. And each of these production plants and sectors had their own directors, and that's why my position was general director. And together, we were the board of directors, and each of these directors were in charge of their respective segment of work. I was the general director until June 1996. And now, I am in the position of the director of Prijedorka. This is a brick factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. There is a mistake on the transcript apparently. Page 38, line 16 to 17. There it reads: "I was appointed the president of the management board after this long discussion which lasted for over one hour and a half." I believe you testified one year and a half.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. One hour and a half. It was the interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, who removed you from that position with the Ljubija mine in June 1996?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back, and I say that I have already stated once that already at the end of 1992, there were attempts to remove me from my position. I was on the list of those 12 directors in Prijedor that the SDS was supposed to remove when the president of the municipality was removed from his position. And then I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't ask you about 1992. The question was: Who removed you in June 1996?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This confirms that they succeeded in 1996. It was the SDS that removed me finally in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you were given that position in 1991, was it -- were you a candidate of the SDS? In other words, did the SDS approve in some way your obtaining that position? Was it part of the division of positions between the three national parties?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said, and you will excuse me for having to give you more details in order to make myself clear. I've already said that I was not a member of the SDS before October 1993. I said a little while ago that my appointment was by the workers' council of the Ljubija mine which at that time, according to the statute, was in charge of that. All the three parties were brought before a fait accomplis. And I must say that the parties had different other candidates, but these people did not apply for the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have many other areas. I don't know if Your Honour wants me to proceed for another few minutes or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You can proceed for another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, regarding the areas of the Ljubija mine company, we have a little map I'd like to have distributed. It's from annex 7 of Mr. Sebire's report. While it's being distributed, I'd just like you, sir, to mark on the map the actual land areas, the property holdings of the Ljubija mine company that appear on that map. You could use, sir, the big red marker that's in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This will be provisionally marked S396.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you could outline -- you have to use the one to your right, sir, to mark on.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. This is a very small map, and I believe this is also a very old shot. I can only tell you in very rough outlines. This is the central mine of the Ljubija local commune, and the management was located roughly in this area. The excavations -- the pits were about 3 kilometres to the south, south of Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, the pits that you're talking about, about how much land area are we talking about -- excuse me, let me withdraw the question. I think it wasn't very precise. Does the company actually own land in the Ljubija area?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When, with the assistance of geological methods, suitable land is found, then there is a public debate about expropriation of this particular area. And all citizens take part in this debate, all citizens who live in the area as well as representatives of the municipality on whose territory the land in question lies. Following debate, the land is expropriated so that exploitation of the land could begin. If there is no agreement on the just compensation between the Ljubija iron ore mine and the owner, then the municipal committee is in charge of making the final decision concerning the expropriation and the appropriation -- the subsequent appropriation of the land.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: These excavations, would it be correct to say that they take place between Ljubija going south to -- on the map we see Rijeka. It says "ST." I don't know if that means Stari Rijeka. There's a road going from Ljubija towards the south to Rijeka. Would it be correct that the excavations occur along this road and on the sides of this road?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's indisputable. If you pay close attention, and I believe you can read this map, this area here, the area I've just marked, you can see different levels, different shafts of floors. This is the central mine heading further south towards Stari Rijeka. Just before you reach Stari Rijeka and to the left, I'll try to mark it with dots again, you have the shafts, the excavations of the southern mines. I did make a mistake yesterday. I called this whole area the southern mines. And you can see that there was mining activity here in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now if now the witness could be shown the same map with a couple of sites marked as they are on annex 7 and distribute that. And for the record, the witness, as he was speaking about the excavation site, made several red dots on the previous exhibit. And Your Honour, may this receive another exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The next one would be S397 provisionally. The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have another comment with respect to this provisionally marked exhibit, Your Honour. With respect to the question that appears on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you have any objection or do you have a comment?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, for the provisional marking, this annex 7 is already admitted as part of Mr. Sebire's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number S281.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So only if you have objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have a comment on the translation, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. On page 42 when counsel asked the question, the answer that's quoted by the witness seems to be answering it's indisputable period to that question. In fact, I think if we check the transcripts, it would be slightly different, although I would hate to impose my view of what the witness said. But then he proceeded to say that it's indisputable this is where he felt the area was as opposed answering the question that it's indisputable. I just want to make it for the record. We can always go back and check it. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we all under the meaning of the answer. But please, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, would it be correct that the two boxes marked on this map Redak, in English "mass gravesite," and Jakorina Kos, mass gravesite, that these gravesite that were excavated are in the area where your company the Ljubija company was mining?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ljubija iron ore mine did dig for iron ore mine in this area throughout the period between 1976 and 1986. Am I allowed to make any further marks on this map? In this area just south of Ljubija, there is Damusa, which is another source of the so-called basic ore, the Siderite ore. And this production line was in operation until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what a "JOY" machine is?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a type of drill, I think American-produced, and it was used to drill mine pits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would it be correct that with a JOY machine, you can drill circular holes through rock?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a type of equipment used to measure the radius of the explosive, and then you drill a hole. Now, the diameter of the hole depends on what we refer to as the "crown" which is placed on the equipment used to drill the hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How many JOY machines were there in Prijedor Municipality between 1992 and 1993 to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the old drill that was obtained, the JOY drill, was purchased in the 1970s, and then there was also the Ingersoll Rand [phoen] drill that was purchased in the 1980s. So I know of two drills that are more or less of the same kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would you expect, sir, that these would be the only two drills in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain about the two at the mine, that they were there. And I think they still are. As far as the town of Prijedor, I really cannot know that because there were people around at that time who were in a position to obtain such drills privately through their own channels. It's just that I don't know these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question before the break. How much does one of those machines cost? How much would it cost in German marks in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I don't know. But at the time they were purchased, if my memory serves me right, I think they cost about 180.000 dollars, American dollars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until half past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.14 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated. Mr. Koumjian, you may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me whether if at any time in which you were a manager or director of the Ljubija mines the equipment of the mines was used, to your knowledge, for burying bodies or hiding bodies of persons who had been killed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a set of photographs, if I could just have the usher please retrieve them from Defence counsel as I gave them to him to look at. And if they could be shown -- I can just check the order -- if they can be shown to the witness. I would ask the usher to put them on the ELMO, and the witness can either look at the screen or at the photographs which would be to his right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you are aware of an exhumation at a site known as Jakorina Kos in September of 2001. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I heard this on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the photograph just zoom out a little bit. Thank you.
