utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph as the site? Have you seen that site, Jakorina Kos, where bodies were exhumed in 2001 and identified as having died in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By looking at this photograph, my conclusion is that these are old mining sites, but if I simply look at the photograph, I can't tell you that this is Jakorina Kos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Can we just go to the photograph on the bottom of the same page. It might be easier just to move the photograph up. Again, sir, do you have any comment? Do you recognise the site or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these craters at the top of the slope?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't offer any comment. Again, these are probably old mining sites from before, and the lay of the land is hilly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Can the next photograph be shown, the next page. Perhaps to speed things up, we can just zoom out to show both photographs at the same time. Sir, just to speed things along, do you recognise anything in these photographs? Or if you would like to make any comment, you may.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to notice anything in particular. In the upper photograph, I think I see a person doing something. I don't see what exactly the person is doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And the lower photograph just appears to be a photograph of soil of various colours. Can we move now to the next photograph, the next page. I'm going to ask you to just look at the next three photographs, have them displayed, and then I'll ask you a question. For the record, we can have the ERN numbers read out for the record. I can't see it right now. Maybe the usher can read it. The ERN number appears to be 02129893. Can we show the next photograph. And it appears to be a boulder and someone has put a stick through the boulder in a hole that runs through the boulder. The second photograph has the ERN number 02130308, again showing a boulder with at least two holes visible. And then the third photograph, please, there's two photographs on this page, 02129883. And then the one I'm more interested in is 02129889. Can that be moved up so we can see the whole photograph? The bottom photograph, please. Which depicts a circular hole in either ground or rock. Sir, in these three -- the last photograph we just looked at and on the two previous pages, we saw circular holes of approximately -- I'm not going to guess the diameter. But maybe 15 centimetres, it appears to be. Sir, are these holes consistent with the holes drilled by a JOY machine?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll comment on the first photograph, the one I had a look at. When mining was being done on a massive scale, the Ingersoll Rand [phoen] drill is used to drill holes up to a depth of 12 to 13 metres and the height of the level is 10 metres. This is a mass of rock which is not homogenous between the slate rocks, a different type of rock that's usually much softer. It often happens, and I'm talking about the first photograph after the mines are laid, after the explosive are inserted, the hole of the explosive in the way miners call it "blows out" which means that the rock doesn't break apart. But instead, what occurs is what we saw in the upper zone of the slate while the drill was drilling. There was a hole left in the upper layer and bits were blown out from down beneath it. Just to help with the diameter, I know that the crowns that we used to -- on top of the equipment, the drills were 120 centimetres wide. As far as the next photograph is concerned, when a massive amount of explosives is laid, large pieces of rocks break off after the explosion which can be scooped up with the digger. So then we do what we refer to as secondary mining. And the rock is drilled, the explosive is laid into the rock, and then the hole is covered with clay. It often happens that the mine itself, the explosive blows out, as we call it, and the big boulders don't simply break into pieces. Now, the last two photographs, the upper section of the page, you see what we refer to as the lone rocks. So if they are in the way of the overall mining project, they are just removed through secondary mining. And if they are not in the way, they are just left where they were. In this second phase, second stage of mining, of secondary mining, another thing that can occur is that a crater is created by the drill itself. You have the diameter of 120 centimetres in the lower layer of the drilled hole itself, and I suppose the lower photograph is a result of exactly such process of mining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you saying centimetres or millimetres?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, millimetres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, the photographs that you saw of these holes, I gather, then are consistent with activities that would have been done by mining equipment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm only judging on the basis of these photographs, so I can't judge clearly. I'm under the impression that I'm taking a mining exam here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I think you're doing well on the exam. Sir, can you tell us based on your knowledge, in 1993, were you aware of bodies and body parts being moved from other locations to Jakorina Kos, the site which is depicted on the map you saw this morning using equipment from the Ljubija mines?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. I certainly didn't know about that. And in my role, in my position, I certainly couldn't know. If what you say is correct, it certainly wasn't information that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, the information that has been presented to this Court is that 373 body and body parts were recovered from that site, and that there was evidence of military explosives and other evidence that the military had been present. Were you aware of the army of Republika Srpska putting bodies in Jakorina Kos in 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony, I have already said, if I remember correctly, that we handed over all the mining explosives to the army as early as the end of 1991. I'm not aware that the army had any activities nor when these activities took place. What I can tell you is that there are two or roads by which you can reach Jakorina Kos. Jakorina Kos I think is about 18 or 20 kilometres from Prijedor, but I really don't know of any military activities, of any activities carried out by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you have a good relationship, a good understanding, with the military in Prijedor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent some time in the Prijedor garrison in 1991. I was there two or three times. When the JNA moved -- started moving from Slovenia and later at some point, I'm not sure, from Croatia, they asked me to find a way to put these people up. The location of this accommodation was determined. It was to be the Mrakovica Hotel on Mount Kozara. They would usually spent a day or two there and then they would proceed with their journey. Later, I did not have any contacts with the army because the garrison, specifically its commander, Arsic, left for the front in Slavonia. I'm not sure where exactly, but I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After the Omarska camp was opened at the end of May 1992, did you have a good relationship with the army? Did you have --

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any sort of contact with the army throughout that period. As I said in my testimony, I once mentioned this, that at the entrance to the municipal building, I heard that people were asking for the ultimatum deadline to turn over weapons to be postponed. And nearby, there were security people from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you wear a uniform in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late May of 1992, for the first 10 or 15 days, yes, I was wearing uniform. I was wearing a gun, too, BT short-barrel rifle, Zastava was the make of the rifle. That was for personal safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would you say as the head of the largest enterprise in Prijedor in 1992, that you cooperated and had a good relationship and understanding with both the military that was conducting operations in places like Kozarac and the municipal leadership?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no cooperation at all with the army at that time. And as far as the leadership of the municipality is concerned, I did a couple of times go to see the secretary for the economy, not very often, though. In view of the fact that he was the minister who was my superior, who in charge of my area of work, his name was Ranko Travar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Using the assets of the Ljubija mine company, did you assist the army in 1992 in order to reach their political agenda, their political goals?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was mobilising, commandeering equipment from the iron ore mine. There are documents. There are mobilisation lists containing this information. I know that bulldozer DO8 was commandeered. I know that at a later stage, some of the vehicles, some of the freight vehicles and some of the buses, used to transport soldiers from the town to the front line were also commandeered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: But your testimony is you yourself did not provide any assistance to the army or cooperation with them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my testimony. Privately and personally, I did not cooperate in any way, but there was no way for me to stand up against mobilisation or the army's commandeering of equipment. There was no way for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to -- let me just ask you one more question on this subject to be clear. Did you use the assets of the Ljubija mine company that were not mobilised or expropriated, did you use that to assist the army?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. There is a document from 1992 in which I am accused of having expropriated part of the funds and then of having forwarded these funds to Serbia. In order to make this right, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about expropriating money yourself; I'm asking about the assets of the mine company --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, to correct the interpretation, I don't think that this gentleman mentioned funds, but equipment. But you can clarify it with the witness. And secondly, let the witness finish his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's first try to find a clarification. On the transcript it reads that your answer was: "There is a document from 1992 in which I am accused of having expropriated part of the funds, and then of having forwarded these funds to Serbia." Could you please correct or state if it's correctly reflected on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My testimony was that towards the end of 1992, I was accused of having expropriated equipment from the mine, and then of having forwarded this equipment, having sent this equipment to Serbia. I'm saying this because there is recorded footage, a tape, on which you can see all the equipment at the mine that had been commandeered. It was stored in hangars and in maintenance halls. And I think that was your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification of this term. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, the reason I stopped you is because I'm not -- my question does not deal with any accusations of you misappropriating property or money. My question is simply: As the head of the largest enterprise in Prijedor, did you use that position and the assets of your company to assist the army? Was your company important for the army's operations in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite specifically, aside from the equipment that had been commandeered, no other equipment was at any time used by the army, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I now would ask -- Mr. Ostojic would like to make a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please no comment, only objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Obviously. Although I accept the OTP's invitation, I think the witness said "mobilised." Commandeered. I mean, we don't want to quibble over it. We would just ask the Court, if at all possible if there could be some level -- or added level of concentration because the words may become important. The witness clearly said it. We could look at the videotape. The Defence is using an enormous amount of restraint from jumping up every 5 seconds to make these objections. So we would ask the Court with all due respect if possible -- and these are words that may ultimately be important in our briefs and final arguments. But I think the witness used the word "mobilised," and it is translated by differently translators always, but it should be consistent since that's the only way you could possible translate that word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please give us some guidance. You are making reference to page and line number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Page 53, line 3, the first word.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Page 53, line 3, the word "commandeered" appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's 4, isn't it? I'm looking at LiveNote sorry. May I ask the booth, was there any misunderstanding? And second, may I ask the witness, it reads now on the transcript, quite specifically "Aside from the equipment that had been commandeered, no other equipment was at any time used by the army." The word "commandeered," did you use this word? I know it's difficult for the translation, retranslation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me just wait. What is the comment by the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My comment concerning this is that according to laws and regulations, the army mobilised part of the equipment of the Ljubija iron ore mine "mobilised." So there are mobilisation lists where a certain piece of equipment is listed as having been mobilised by the army. And which from that moment on is under the control of the army. What I can say is that no other equipment that I knew of was being used by the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the purposes of -- at least the attempt to facilitate our work, may I ask the booth in case there may be a word which has -- or might have two similar or different meanings, that they draw our attention to this. And if necessary, even ask what is the meaning of the word, what did you want to say. Otherwise, I think we will end up in a mess. And I know all of our work is extremely difficulty. We are working not only in three languages; we have an addition of at least three other languages in this courtroom. But we have to overcome these obstacles. And therefore I invite you in doubt, let us know from the side of the booths. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you repair equipment for the army in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that part of the transportation means were being repaired in the central workshop in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask the booth to play a video that has been prepared. It was S11, but it's a specific extract -- excerpt from that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we use the time when the video is prepared --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's ready. Then please, it may be started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, there will be a video in front of you being played, I'll ask you to listen to the video, and then I'll ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You may play the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can we stop. Stop, please. I don't believe -- the translation does not need to be on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could this please be rewound that we can follow on the basis of the translation. I take it that is a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies to everyone. That was my error. The translation had not yet been handed out. If everyone is ready, we can start again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The largest iron ore mine in our country, the Ljubija mines, has suffered certain consequences as a result of the war in the area of Prijedor municipality and of the overall situation that prevails not only in the Autonomous Region of Krajina, but generally in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia. The mine used to cooperate with foreign companies, both in the area of procurement, spare parts, and exports of ore. Due to a combination of circumstances, it all stopped. There are no payments and no transport of ore to the steel works in Zenica and Smederevo. Nevertheless, in the past two months, the mine managed to overcome its problems. It even paid the salaries and placed some of its assets at the disposal of the military authorities and the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We are talking now about specific issues with Ostoja Marjanovic, manager of the Ljubija mines. "Let me first point out that the principal activity of the mine has been suspended, and that is the mine production. It goes out saying that it was caused by recent events, the war and wartime conditions, and severed communications. Consequently, we are not able to deliver our products any longer to Zenica of Smederevo. But, in view of the events that took place after the 22nd of May, we are making efforts, just like all other economic entities are doing more or less successfully, to meet the requirements and demands of this particular moment. First, we started food production in our catering facilities. I must praise our employees who did their duty and came to work, even during the curfew. "You happened to have some stocks that proved to be invaluable at the time of need while the war operations were in progress. "Well, that is a fact. That was really true. But I don't think that it should be overemphasised. It seems...we had anticipated something like that to happen, irrespective of other circumstances. And we had some stocks that helped us get through the initial stage when we lacked working capital needed for the procurement of foodstuffs. This is one of the segments that we worked on. Another segment involved putting the central metal processing workshop into operation, and it started doing repair work on the military equipment, the equipment of other work organisations, and eventually our own equipment that we had used for reconstruction of the town. You know very well what happened, that there was demolition, et cetera. Now, if you walk through certain parts of Prijedor, you cannot recognise them because of those dilapidated and demolished houses. But we have rehabilitated the area with our machinery and our men. "I wouldn't miss an opportunity to mention that the catering service of the Ljubija mines has taken a huge burden on their shoulders, and they still do, thanks to their stocks, but also with good cooperation of Prijedor's wholesalers and the supplier from Banja Luka, Veleprehrana, with whom they had a purchasing contract signed earlier. I also must give credit to the metal workers of Prijedor who managed in these times of war to meet all the requirements of the barracks and the war brigade in Prijedor. "Well, let us go back a little. You mentioned that the salaries were paid. That was for April of this year, and it was possible solely thanks to the Smederevo metallurgical complex. The amount paid in salaries were 450 million dinars, I mean old dinars. It was an investment, in fact, in future production and we managed to make this payment. When you spoke about cooperation, I think that we need to mention everyone, retailers and Veleplrehrana, and -- who financed a greater part of our operation, because they supplied a lot of material in the beginning. We also had good cooperation with all other enterprises from Prijedor. I estimate that there's a high level of understanding between us and the military and exceptionally good cooperation with the local leadership of Prijedor Municipality. I do not think that Ljubija deserves to be specially highlighted because it fits into the mosaic of joint efforts to create this new system which is our goal."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, just a few questions about your last comment. You said that the efforts of the Ljubija mine "fits into the mosaic of joint efforts to create this new system which is our goal." First, when you say "our goal," whose goal were you talking about? Who did you mean by "our"?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goal of the Ljubija mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And what was these joint efforts to create this new system? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may object to the form of the question, Your Honour. On the translation itself they have a question mark by that word, and it wasn't interpreted. I know the booth is reading for its convenience the translation offered by the OTP. But I don't know that they gleaned from the actual video that that was the word. So I just want that to be clear on the question, that it's OTP's contention that that's what the word is but they themselves have placed a question mark on that word. And the booth merely read -- and I'm not sure if they placed a question mark -- I'm not sure if they translated the video at the same time it was being played or merely read from it. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me just briefly comment, Your Honour. First of all, the Defence has many times pointed to the amount of time the cross-examination takes. I hope the interruptions are not counted against us by the Defence. As far as this witness's use of the word, he listened in his own language and he understood my question because he had listened to the tape and the word he had used. If counsel wants to correct the word, I don't have a problem. If you want to use another word rather than "system," I'll accept the other word.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We can ask -- go ahead, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't remember the word any more, but we could hear it, and maybe the witness can repeat that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the witness has listened to the tape and not read that what we had before us, and apparently it was read out in English. And therefore, I think the witness knows what it's all about. Therefore, please proceed, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you said, sir, that "I do not think that Ljubija deserves to be specially highlighted because it fits into the mosaic of joint efforts," joint efforts by who, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to point out two things when it comes to your question. We're talking about the end of April when this interview was done. We provided services to everybody, and people paid us for these services. I said in this interview that the mining operation had stopped, that the payment transactions were not in place, that we could not bank with the banks in Sarajevo and Zenica. We had contact with Smederevo. We didn't expect that the interruption on the roads to Smederevo would last that long. That's why we had to create the conditions to be able to pay the salaries to our employees. I have to point out that at that time, there was such a situation that put me and some of the people into the position, those of us who did not agree with the referendum that had taken place, and only the -- the only people -- there were only two people that took part in the referendum and the third people were not asked any questions. At that time, I wanted us to stay in Yugoslavia, and that is what I meant. When I said, this I wanted to remain in Yugoslavia because Yugoslavia for me was always and at that time still was, it remained it very good option.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir, you referred to the date of this interview having taken place in April. During the interview, just to remind you stated -- excuse me?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. During the interview, you say that, I'm reading from the bottom of page 18, around six lines up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, we tried to understand the date. Where did you take the date from? On page 18, second-last paragraph, it reads: "The events that took place after 22 May."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm bringing to the witness's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry for this confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Couple points.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...the witness. We're not going to hold this against the OTP in terms of their time. But we're looking at Exhibit S11 that was submitted with the translation which has specifically has pages 12 to 14. On the very top of that exhibit that we would ask the Madam Registrar to show for us on the ELMO, it specifically shows the date of when this interview was in Banja Luka, so -- production by Banja Luka. And for the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We shouldn't interfere too much. And I apologise myself for having interrupted the line of questions prepared by the Prosecution during cross-examination. It's the right of the party to take their own approach to come to this goal. So no objections admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have another objection, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We never received this document, never. Not the videotape, not the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The document is admitted as S11 long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's what we're trying to clarify if we would just be permitted --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll clarify for counsel. It's 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, the Prosecution is trying to clarify this, and as we allowed the Defence to develop how it comes to this date, what is the date, is the date correct? So it's for the Prosecution to follow this line of questions prepared, and I formally apologise for having interrupted you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for Defence counsel, the 65 ter number of the entire tape is 798. The earlier smaller portion was played, and it's a video -- the ERN number is 0000444.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, just to assist you with the date of this interview, you indicated, as His Honour pointed out, that you talked about at one point events that took place after the 22nd of May. And you also talk about demolitions in Prijedor. Were there demolitions in Prijedor in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a mistake. I could not see that on this footage that you showed me. I couldn't see the time. I'm here talking about the repairs in town after the war operations. I am rather tired, so I missed that. I must say that the war operations, especially in the area of Berek, on the 30th of May when there was this attack on Prijedor, there were houses that had been set fire to in the war operations. Some of the houses in the town centre were also demolished. And later on in the main street, in the town centre, one of the houses was set on fire. A body was set up in the municipality that was in charge of making repairs in that part of the city. And that body hired some of the equipment from the mines in order to be able to carry out that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And that would have been in June of 1992. Correct? Or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in this interview, you talked about having a high level of understanding between you and the military. Why is it you said this when you told us that the military had forcibly taken over the Omarska facility from you and that that is something that you would have opposed even at the risk of your own life?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just said that this cooperation was good in terms of them paying services to us, and the services in question are the repairs of their transportation means in our central workshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, how many people, how many friends and colleagues of yourself disappeared from the Omarska camp, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my answer cannot be direct. After these events which took place on the 30th of May, and during the month of June, we didn't know who was -- who would be turning up for work except for those who were under work obligation as indicated based on the documents, for those who were on the list for the 5th and the 6th of May. When I communicated to my subordinate managers that we should have all the people reporting for work on the 1st of each month, there was actually no work, but we needed to know who of the work force was still available to us. Once that was established, I issued a document firing some of the people irrespective of their ethnic background. I believe that I signed about 1600 such documents firing people. And the question that you have just put to me, I really don't know, and there was no way for me to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, didn't you learn that Mr. Sakib Islamovic who you mentioned in your testimony as a colleague you worked with was put into the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sakib Islamovic, when he returned from Omarska, I heard that he had returned. I sent him some cigarettes to his apartment. It was only then that I found out that he had been in Omarska from which he returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a photograph I'd like to be shown to counsel. It is ERN number -- to counsel and to the witness and the Court. ERN number 00356464.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: While this is done, may I ask the OTP, do you want to tender these photographs separately or following the other coloured photos under S15?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think it might make more sense to give them one additional number, and then consecutively numbered after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then this would be S397, and -1 following in the order it has been shown and it still is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in the photograph that's now on the screen, would I be correct in assuming that you are the individual in the right-hand side of the photograph looking sideways in the background?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The person with his arm around the gentleman in the middle, the person to your right in the photograph is Mr. Slobodan -- Mr. Balaban - I forget his first name - that you mentioned earlier today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of the other two individuals.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan's arm is around Smail Zahirovic. Next to him is Ibro Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court the occupations and the positions prior to the takeover of the municipality of Prijedor on the 30th of April of Mr. Zahirovic and Mr. Paunovic? Did they work for the Ljubija mine?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. I believe that Ibro Paunovic was the director of the mining centre, and Mr. Zahirovic was the director of protection and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever learn that these colleagues of yours were killed in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all the events, they didn't turn up for work. I didn't know that they were killed. I suppose that this is what happened because I haven't heard of their lot to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe in your testimony, you mentioned Mr. Mehmedalija Sarajlic. Can you tell us his position?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember ever having mentioned Mehmedalija Sarajlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Mr. Sarajlic -- I accept, sir -- I realise I made a mistake. You did not mention Mr. Sarajlic, and I apologise to counsel and to you. You know Mr. Sarajlic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what his position was with the Ljubija mine.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say because when I was appointed director, I offered him to be the director of the mining and construction works. He was a construction engineer. He refused that. He continued working in his office without the position that he had occupied previously. And previously, he was a member of the management board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You also mentioned in your testimony Mr. Esref Crnkic. If counsel would like, I can find that reference if it's necessary. Sir, do you recall mentioning Mr. Crnkic? Do you know who Mr. Crnkic is?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I have mentioned him, and when you say his name, I don't recognise it. Does he have a first name?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe - and forgive my pronunciation - Esref Crnkic.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now your pronunciation was better. Esref Crnkic, I did mention him. I said that he was a director of repairs and maintenance, and that his office served for the meetings of the SDA Executive Board. And I also said that the central workshop stopped working on the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that both Mr. Sarajlic and Mr. Crnkic were killed in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, on the 30th -- prior to the 30th of April of 1992, you were one of the most prominent citizens of Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I cannot give you any opinions about myself or how people perceived me. It is up to the people of Prijedor to say that. Can I please ask the Honourable Court, I'm very tired. I'm finding it very difficult to concentrate, if I can have a short break. I would kindly ask you for a break. I am 60 years of age, and I feel tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No additional explanation is needed. Let's have a break until 10 minutes to 3.00. But in the meantime, let's just decide on the admission of evidence first. We had the pictures. Objections related to the pictures? None.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence under S397-1 and following. Then, the following picture would be this one, S398. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, S398. Then we have the video. This will be far more difficult. We are aware that in the past, another clip of the same video was admitted into evidence as S11. It's the Prosecution who tendered this document. May I ask, do you want to have this as a special clip with a new exhibit number or would you prefer to have it as S11-1?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: S11-1 is fine. I just want to make it as easy as possible for someone going through the transcript to find the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour. We would like to clarify the point if we may. We can either try to do that now or after the break, whatever the Court desires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's quite clear, and I may anticipate what you want to say. We are aware that we are discussing a production of TV Banja Luka from the 30th of June, 1992. And this is part of the transcript admitted into evidence as S11A, but there only pages 12 to 14. And this is another part of this same translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, it's that and two other points in connection with that document, Your Honour, that I'd like to raise if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I suggest the witness be excused if he's tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I thought it might be relaxing to follow the dispute amongst the parties. Of course, you're excused. And may I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. Thank you. So please, no additional problems, I think. When we -- what is your objection, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the objection is that the representations we believe that were made in connection with Exhibit S11 were specifically for that portion of the tape, and therefore although we insisted on getting the entire transcript presented to us in written form, they suggested that they were only going to confine it to this segment of it. We were not given at any time these new pages 18 through 21 of the tape that they perceive now is part of S11. We want to know why. We want the remaining pages, the 12 pages before the Banja Luka tape that they used as well as the subsequent pages following page 20 of this new exhibit. We thought and believe that the Court's ruling - and we could be wrong on this - was to provide the Defence in its totality the evidence that they have. And not to piecemeal, withhold information and to give us the information as they so deemed fit. We would at this time request if permitted to have the entirety of the translated version of that videotape because we would like to also analyse the videotape. Without making prejudgement, there were some tapes that overlapped in terms of the time period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear the comments given by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the videotape in question was disclosed to the Defence on the 25th of March of last year. If counsel wants a -- if the translation and apparently the translation was not provided, I don't know whether or not it was available that date. But we'll happily provide the rest of the translation. The Defence does speak the language, and given the -- that we haven't received any translation of the Defence documents, I think they understand that sometimes translations can take a long period of time. But the tape was provided almost a year ago in their language, the entire tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we appreciate that. The tape was provided. The representation was that this segment with the accompanying translation would be given to us. Clearly, if only that segment was provided - again, I don't want to speculate, I don't mean to infer anything to the OTP - how could it be possible that they would have numbered those pages 12 through 14 unless someone at some point would have presumed that there was other translations or was it hypothetical on their part that there were going to be 12 pages preceding that and many pages following these 18, 19, and 20. Secondly, I would encourage us to listen to those videotapes so that we could, I think, make a determination whether or not the audiosound of those tapes are adequate enough so that despite the fact that you might be bilingual that it is very, very difficult unless you have sophisticated equipment to pick up the questions and responses and issues that are raised during some of these interviews. I invite the Court to do and that we could all do it together if the Court permits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think that the exhibit as such is in its entirety in the position of the Defence, and I believe the same is true for the Chamber. So it shouldn't be a problem. And please feel free whenever you believe the translation, we can read "rough English version," for example, on S11A. So please, draw our attention to these points. In addition, I believe the Prosecution can't do more than provide the entire text. And apparently, we have transcripts in B/C/S as we had it with the document S11B. So it's even far more easier to follow that what can be heard from the video. And the English translation, and the Judges would appreciate also to get copies of this -- of the English version at least in case there might be a problem related to the language. With the assistance of booth and Judge Vassylenko, we will try to resolve the problems. It's now only the questions first, are there any other objections as a matter of principle for the admitting into evidence of this concrete part?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would go as S11-1. And the transcript in English, S11-1-a. In the B/C/S, to be followed, S11-1-b.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, an unrelated point to this exhibit but related to the witness, during our proffer of the witness we were informed, although did not extract that information because we didn't think it was relevant, but just so the Court and the OTP knows, this witness has recently undergone kidney surgery, and we invite the Court to ask him, because I think that's some of the problems why he's having a little bit of an endurance issue and is having a lack of concentration in connection with his testimony here. So we would just like, and perhaps it was an omission on our part, so we should have asked him ahead but we didn't think his personal medical condition may be relevant to the facts in the indictment. But we think it's important at least to note that, and that's why I think he's experiencing especially late in the afternoon some of the problems that we've seen here. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We would appreciate that we would be informed at the beginning of a hearing on these problems. Any other issues during this point in time in the absence of the witness? This is apparently not the case. The trial stays adjourned until 3.00 sharp. And may we please, the witness be informed on this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask the witness, whenever you feel uncomfortable, please let us know immediately as you did in the past that we can take the necessary steps. And a second point that I don't forget, I shouldn't forget to announce if you do not know yet, the meetings -- the hearing tomorrow, Thursday, the 6th, and Friday the 7th will take place as scheduled but in Courtroom III. So Mr. Koumjian, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in your testimony, you mentioned the names of several other prominent individuals in Prijedor that you knew. For example, Mr. Silvija Seric went with you, I believe, on -- it was part of the peace organisation. Dr. Esad Sadikovic, who came the president of that movement, was elected president of that movement. And you mentioned Dr. Minka Cehajic, your neighbour, and I presume you also knew her husband, the president of the municipality, Dr. -- excuse me, Professor Cehajic. Is that correct, you knew all of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know all of these people. Of course, they lived in Prijedor. I lived in Prijedor, too. We lived together in the same town. Silvester Seric was the president of the SDZ. He was not a member of the peace movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm sorry. I apologise, but can we use the term the president of the Municipal Assembly for Mr. Cehajic instead of president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we all know what is meant, and we shouldn't try to be too sophisticated. Sometimes all of us make this -- I wouldn't call it a mistake, but we all know what was meant. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that all three of these individuals were killed or disappeared in the Omarska camp, the camp that was -- or the facilities owned by the Ljubija mine in 1992, that they disappeared in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to state thing. Please try to understand me correctly. After those events, news arrived, but from the streets. Certain names were mentioned. They said that these people had been killed. After the events, unfortunately [as interpreted], I did meet some of those people who had been referred to as dead, and they were still alive. It's very difficult for me to learn now after all this time that some of these people are actually missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If the witness can clarify whether he said unfortunately or fortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can come back. But please, let the witness speak out in its entirety as it was requested by your side previously. So you're making reference to line 16 on page 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And no doubt, it should read "fortunately" instead of "unfortunately."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, my question dealt with Mr. Seric, Dr. Sadikovic, and Muhamed Cehajic. Did you see any of these three people alive after they entered the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we understood each other correctly. I did not see these specific people. What I said was that word about Prijedor was that certain people had gone missing. And yet, at some later time I found, fortunately, that those people were, in fact, still alive. It is very difficult for me to look at these names, names of colleagues of mine, from the iron ore mine also, look at these names and hear what happened to those people because I was living in the hope that these things would not prove true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, I gather from your answer that you were somewhat surprised today to learn about some of this information. Isn't it correct that you testified on the first day of your testimony about a murder that occurred in May in Prijedor. And I'm referring to page 25 of the transcript of the 3rd of February. You were asked on line 10: "Did you hear whether the police killed someone in order to retaliate, to take revenge for this murder?" Your answer was: "No, I'm sure this didn't happen. Because since I heard about the murder of this policeman, I would have heard about other events had they occurred in Prijedor." So, sir, why was it that you were certain that you would have heard about murders, any retaliation for the murder of this policeman, but you are saying that you did not know about the murder or the killing of these extremely prominent people that you knew?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we have not understood each other very well. That is not what I said. I will repeat now what I said. Word was about town that people had gone missing, and the list of names included these names, but there were other names that people were talking about as having gone missing, too. Only after all these events, I met certain people among people who had been talked about as having gone missing. For example, there was news about Mr. Sakib, that he had been hurt. Fortunately, he came out and left. I refused to believe that those people were gone, that they had gone missing. I hoped they were still alive. And fortunately, I must say again, that I was very pleased to see again that the people were in fact still alive. And it's very difficult for me to face the facts now as stated by you that certain people are still missing and no longer with us. As for events from May 1992, I think it was in mid-May, it's becoming very difficult for me to focus, I'm talking about the period after that, and then up to about the 20th of May, that was the period I referred to when I said I didn't hear anything about retaliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about Dedo Crnalic, who you described as your great friend on page 10 of the transcript of the 3rd of February, line 15. You called him a great friend of mine, an eminent sports worker in Prijedor. Did you learn that while being escorted by Prijedor police to Manjaca, that these police slit his throat outside of the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear of that. I don't know -- your question actually, how could I have heard anything like that since I was in Prijedor? And after some of those people went to Manjaca, I don't know which people exactly, all traces were lost. Families were separated, and parts of some families went to Zagreb or to Belgrade. It was difficult to keep track. I really didn't hear anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, help me with this: You've told us that you declared yourself in 1991 a Yugoslav and that you participated and helped start a peace movement. So I gather that you were a person who was aiming for the coexistence of all three nationalities in the municipality of Prijedor, you believed that they could coexist in peace together. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Given that, sir, please help me understand, why is it that in 1993, after the disappearance of all of these individuals, after the Omarska camp appeared on world news following the visit of foreign journalists in August, after what you said was the forcible takeover of that mine by the army, after the events and destruction of Kozarac, Stari Grad, the cleansing of the Brdo region, what you described in your testimony as the exodus of so many people of non-Serb nationality from Prijedor, why is it that in 1993, you then joined the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please hear me out. I will have to elaborate. I declared myself and identified myself as a Yugoslav. The reason was that I was born in that state, and I loved the state of Yugoslavia. The events which occurred in 1991 and 1992 led to secession which caused a great amount of suffering to most of the different ethnic groups. Since 1991, I have continued to be no longer a Yugoslav, but I became nothing in a way, not a Serb and not a Yugoslav. Since most of my people joined together, I stuck with my people, and I'm sorry that part of the people of Prijedor left, be it after having been forced to leave or having left before. For the period of eight months, I thought it would not have been fair for me to be the president of the Executive Board without being a member of the SDS. That was the only reason. And as soon as I resigned after finding myself unable to implement my own policies in the Executive Board, I resigned on the 1st of August. So you see, it lasted for about eight months. This particular Prijedor government lasted for a year. Mr. Travar, who was the president of the Executive Board, also resigned at a later date. I don't know what the circumstances were. But this was the reason, and this provides a more substantial answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Another correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Vice-president --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness said that he left the SDS party the same day he resigned. So -- and it's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the booth, it's 76, line 7. Did the witness add to the sentence "I resigned on the 1st of August" anything?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the question please be restated so we can get this clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that you resigned from the SDS party the same day you resigned as vice-president of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I resigned in writing to my position as the vice-president of the Executive Board. It was not an irrevocable resignation. I told orally the president of the SDS that I wanted to cease being a member, that I wanted out of the party. If I was still on their books, that was their problem. But let me explain why I did not file an irrevocable resignation. I believe that since the assembly elected me, that I would be called upon by the assembly to explain my resignation. I was never invited to the assembly, and I was never given an opportunity to say why I had resigned and why I was leaving the area in which people like Mr. Kurnoga and Mr. Radanovic were moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, Mr. Kurnoga was the president of the municipality when you joined the Executive Board, and Mr. Radanovic, otherwise known as Cigo, was the vice-president. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. You may remember that -- I think I stated yesterday or the day before yesterday, I'm finding it increasingly difficult to keep focussed. I hope to be able to go on. I said that I had insisted on those people resigning from their positions, and that was the condition I imposed for accepting the position of president. These people never resigned, and all my work was about getting these people to resign and bringing new people to their positions. I failed, and that was the reason why I left the Executive Board. I think the transcript must reflect this. That in agreement, with the SDS, there was an understanding that those people would resign.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in the period of 1992, that summer, spring and summer, a great number of the directors of the largest enterprises in Prijedor were dismissed. Correct, by the SDS party? Correct? Excuse me. Let me withdraw the question. By the Crisis Staff, a great number of the directors of the -- of enterprises in Prijedor were dismissed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Can the counsel present such a document in which the Crisis Staff is firing people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it a real question? I would be more than surprised that this would be a real question based on that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From our side or from the Prosecution side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let them present the document that they removed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When something was or is already in evidence, it seems not to be necessary. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Executive Board or Crisis Staff? The question first was? Executive Board? And then the counsel asked about the Crisis Staff. We know about dismissals by the Executive Board, but we are not aware of dismissals by the Crisis Staff, of the directors of the enterprises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would the counsel of Prosecution please be so kind and support this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, but first, let me just state for the record my objection that I shall be allowed to conduct an examination without inference of counsel. They can do re-examination, redirect, but in any event. Your Honour, I have in front of me -- I would like the witness to be shown S86.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As a matter of principle, in future, when a document is already admitted into evidence, it's not a reason for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And please, if the witness can also be shown S46 and S45.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, first if we can go to S86, my question to you was: Were you aware that in the spring and summer of 1992 many directors of leading enterprises in Prijedor were dismissed? And I'd like to mention some of them now, looking at this document. For example, the director of the Kozara Putavi enterprise, Mr. Husein Redzic. The director of Jela industries in Kozarac, number 11, and Zijad Mahmuljin. The director of the Sportska Dvorana Mladost public company, Emir Babic. The director of the 4th of July public company, Jusuf Harambasic. The director of the Kozara tourist socially-owned company, Mehmedalija Kapetanovic. And the director of the Giro Mrakovica socially-owned company, Mirza Beglerbegovic. You're aware that many directors of companies were dismissed in the spring and summer of 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I do know, and I even talked to this man - I'm talking about Mr. Risto Banovic, who is a schoolmate of mine, an old schoolmate of mine. As for the other parts, I am not familiar with this document. I don't know that these things happened. Mr. Redzic, who was also a neighbour of mine, I'm not sure if he left Prijedor before the removal or dismissal. As for the others, to be quite honest, I wasn't thinking about it, and I didn't have any contact with these people who had been dismissed. This was probably done by the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And in fact, you were removed by the SDS party as the head of Ljubija, but not until 1996. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. 1996. But you forgot to mention that I said that towards the end of 1992 and in 1993, there were attempts at my removal, and I was surprised they didn't actually manage when Mr. Kurnoga and the remaining part of the group I've told you about came to power. Why didn't they succeed? I gathered a number of documents on the basis of which they could have the director replaced. There was a rule that had been introduced. If the managing director was not performing his duty competently, if he wasn't taking good care of the company, and if he wasn't being economical in the way he was running the company, but they couldn't pin down any of these elements in my work. If they had managed to, they certainly would have had me dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you could try to keep your answers a little bit shorter, sir, while still completely answering the question, would it be correct, then, that no effort was made to remove you while Dr. Stakic was the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no attempts. I don't know. I said that I did my job in a proper way, and these people - and this is something I mentioned. You should remember this. They said, these people said: "We have the power but we don't have the money." And that was why they requested dismissals. And that's why I came under attack in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned in your testimony the first day the head of the SDK Hava, and I believe you did not recall her last name, but it is Bahtijaragic, correct, who is the head of the SDK before the takeover of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I commented on the session, on the meeting of the businessmen after the takeover. I can't remember the exact date where they were present, and that's when I said that they were present. But I don't remember now. That is the last name. I also referred to the managing director of the -- I referred to Miro, Mr. Miro Turnisek who worked for the Kras company. That's the meeting I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Let me try to refresh your recollection. Sir, isn't it true that Ms. Hava Bahtijaragic, a Muslim, was barred from entering the SDK the day of the takeover and she was replaced by Slobodan Garjanovic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether she was allowed to enter the building and who replaced her. I just talked about the session at which she was present, and Mr. Cehajic was also there and other people. To be honest, I actually left that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually that session you're talking about regarding the redirection of funds from Sarajevo to Banja Luka occurred before the takeover. Isn't that true? Because Mr. Cehajic was still the president of the municipality during that meeting. Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is a misunderstanding. Let me go back to that session. After the takeover when all of these people that I just mentioned were present, I don't know of any such meetings where the redirection of funds would be discussed. I don't know of any such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me move on, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown S46 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Briefly, sir, if you look at the document, it indicates that the Crisis Staff president, signed by Dr. Milomir Stakic, it's forwarding a decision from the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina for implementation. And then if you look at S45, you will see that that is the decision being forwarded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we please have the English documents on the ELMO, please. First, 46, then 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This is 45. Your Honour wanted to see 46 first, I believe. Did Your Honour get to see 46? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, the decision of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff which hopefully you have a copy of in front of you, it ends with the ERN number 633170, yes, if I can briefly read out the first part of the decision. "All executive posts involving a likely flow of information, posts involving the protection of public property, that is, all posts important for the functioning of economy may only be held by the personnel of Serbian nationality. This refers to all socially-owned enterprises, joint stock companies, state institutions, public utilities, ministries of the interior, and the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These posts may not be held by employees of Serbian nationality who have not confirmed by plebiscite or who in their minds have not made it ideologically clear that the Serbian democratic party is the sole representative of the Serbian people." My question for you, sir, is first: In this middle paragraph when it refers to all socially-owned enterprises, joint stock companies, state institutions, would that include in your mind the Ljubija iron ore mines?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that in the heading where it says DPRZR Ljubija, the full title is the state-owned company, the iron ore mines Ljubija. And now the answer to your question is the state-owned company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you receive this decision? Do you recall receiving this decision before you did those dismissals you talked about, about 1600 dismissals you signed?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. I see this decision for the first time in my life. I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S84. If the English could be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, we see that S84 is a decision dated the 2nd of July, 1992, signed "president of the Crisis Staff, Milomir Stakic. Copies to all parties mentioned in the order and files." And the order is in paragraph 1: "All organs, enterprises, and communities are ordered to terminate the employment of workers who have participated in the armed rebellion and who are currently in Omarska and Keraterm." Sir, as a person with experience in government, as the former manager of the largest enterprise in Prijedor, can you tell me would it make sense for this order to be sent to enterprises without a list of those individuals who were imprisoned in Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Can you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You've talked a little bit about Dr. Stakic. In your dealings with him, was he a rational, intelligent person?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was of an average rationality or of an average intelligence. That is all I can say. I do not belong to the profession that could give you a more appropriate answer to that. I'm talking just as a person who knew him, who knows him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in this order signed by Dr. Stakic, the first paragraph: "Orders enterprises," and I presume the Ljubija mine would be considered an organ or enterprise, "to terminate the employment of workers currently in Omarska and Keraterm." Would it make sense to you for Dr. Stakic to send this to an enterprise without informing the enterprise of which workers were in Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how I'm supposed to answer. I don't understand this order. I apologise. Just give me a moment, please. I've read the order, but I do not understand what should be enclosed or what would be logical to have with it. What else would one need to have together with this order? I really don't understand. I don't understand what would be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, it would be logical that you would need to know which of your workers like some of the individuals in the photograph we showed you, the two directors, were in the Omarska camp in order to know who it was you were supposed to fire. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first tell you that I did not have this order. Secondly, let me tell you that I have already stated in my testimony that one or two or three months after the beginning of the crisis, I did what I did, what I had to do. I also have to say that the president of the Executive Board, Mr. Mandic whose first name I cannot recall, he asked me to show him the documents. I did not give them to him. He sent his inspectors, but I thought that this was confidential material, that it was my company's secret. And that is why I reported him to the misdemeanours court, because I didn't allow anybody to interfere with my work, with the things I was doing in order to establish how many people were still on my payroll, how many people I was still supposed to pay salaries to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you receive the information about which of your employees were in the Omarska or Keraterm camp? Can you answer that yes or no. Did you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And your company was at that time the largest employer in Prijedor Municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But again, can you give me the relevant period? Throughout the period starting with the 1980s up to these events, my company did indeed have the largest number of employees. And if my memory serves me well, I believe that I have mentioned it already here in this Court that when I became the director on the 1st of February, 1991, there were 4.630 employees. I've already mentioned that. I don't know whether I have given you the ethnic background, but I believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you're not on trial here. Let me just remind you of that. All I'm asking in these questions, I'm just asking you for the answer to specific questions. Sir, you brought with you to Court, and we saw the first day, a list of several employees who had gone to work on, I believe, the 4th of May. Where did you get those papers from?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that I'm not on trial here. And as for these documents that I have shown to you, I got them from the heads and directors of sectors and departments. All these documents are signed. They are original signatures. But I must say something: Before that time, there was a significant decrease in the rate of production, and a lot of people were on paid leave. They were on standby. A lot of people had moved from Prijedor already in late 1991. I could not -- there was no way for me to check who of the 4.630 people had left, who were on standby. I had to gather some documents, and I had to trust the respective heads of departments and sectors who gave me these documents, who gave me these lists of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. And I'm just going to try to encourage you to limit your answers to the questions because I know you're tired, and if you can concentrate on the question, we can finish sooner. I asked you where you got them from, and you said the directors. When did you receive these documents? In 1992 or more recently?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992. These are original documents bearing original signatures of the persons who drew up those lists, and they bear the original stamps. And this can all be verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You told us that you left the company or were replaced by the SDS in 1996. Why is it, sir, that you maintained possession of these lists of names from 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My file -- when I left the mines, I moved my file, my very huge file - mind you I had spent 30 years in the mines starting with the foreman to the general direction, so I found that in my file. When I spoke in Prijedor with Mr. Lukic, I didn't mention these lists because I was not aware of having them. When I then went home, I inspected my file. I came by those documents, and I deemed that they would be interesting for the Honourable Trial Chamber to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Among the documents that you maintained, did you also maintain the dismissals? I believe -- you can correct me, but I believe you indicated you dismissed 1600 individuals. Do you have records of those signed dismissals?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1.600 times three copies, it's another huge file that can be found in the legal services of the mines. I believe that these documents are still there in the files. So this is something that I did not have at home in my personal file.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm going to leave the subject of employment and move on to a different subject. Sir, you talked about some interactions you had with members of the Crisis Staff in the night shift in the communications centre in the basement of the Prijedor Municipality. Correct? Can you tell us, why were you there?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I would like to say this was not in the communications centre but in the office next to the early warning and information centre. I will tell you exactly why, but don't take this as a joke. I went to play cards. I just went to keep them company and to play cards with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And who were you playing cards with?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Mr. Milomir Stakic, with Mr. -- from the all people's defence, Mr. Slavko Budimir. Kovacevic did not play cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was Dr. Stakic in uniform when you saw him there?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, based upon your experience the next year working for the municipality, how many employees did Prijedor Municipality have?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I really don't know, but there were more employees than in Doboj, and still Doboj was a larger municipality than Prijedor. I can't tell you exactly, but there were over a hundred people working there. But I never knew the exact data. There were six or seven secretariats. In each of them were 25 to 30 people, so you can come by using arithmetic -- so you can come to an approximate figure. I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your testimony is that you believe that the president of the municipality did a night shift to answer the phone about complaints about electricity, water, and roads, that the president of the municipality himself, his job was to answer the phone all night and take these telephone calls?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, he was on call in night shifts on behalf of the Crisis Staff. Whether his post allowed him to do that or not, I don't know. In any case, what I have told you is God's honest truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for clarification, on the transcript, and it was your question, you spoke about the president of the municipality. I think you wanted to say president of the Municipal Assembly or am I incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I will in the future use that term, or president of the Crisis Staff in this particular era, or president of the National Defence Council. We have a number of different titles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I only want to be on the safe side that in future nobody can say that the witness may have maybe referred to the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Assembly, Dr. Stakic, your testimony is, sir, that he took an all-night shift to answer phone calls, complaints about electricity and water, when there were over a hundred employees of the municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were so many employees working in the morning shift, in the first shift. And this is the on-call duty during the night, between 10.00 in the evening and the morning. And I've already told you that I would arrive there around 9.00 in the evening, and I would come back around midnight, never later than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked some questions about the statute of the municipality and the role of the president of the Municipal Assembly in that statute. Can you tell me, are you aware of anything in the statute of Prijedor Municipality, the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the law of Yugoslavia that would indicate that a minority of deputies, 28, could forcibly take over the assembly and expel the majority from different nationalities?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that. This is a legal issue. But this is what happened. That is what happened on the 30th of April, there was a takeover.
